The first thing the town lost was the sound of its clock.

For ninety-three years, the clock above the railway station had struck every hour with a note so deep that people claimed they could feel it through the soles of their shoes. Then, one Tuesday in October, the mechanism stopped. Nobody saw it happen. At eleven, the bell had sounded. At noon, there was only traffic, rainwater slipping through gutters, and a dog barking at a delivery van. Most people assumed they had been distracted. By evening, everyone knew. The hands remained fixed at seventeen minutes past eleven.

The council put up a notice explaining that repairs would begin as soon as a specialist could be found. Specialists, it turned out, were scarce. The company that had built the mechanism no longer existed, and its last apprentice had retired to an island where he repaired boats and refused to answer emails. A newer clock could be installed, someone suggested. This proposal generated forty-seven letters, two public meetings, and an argument outside the bakery that nearly ended a friendship of thirty years. Meanwhile, the old clock continued displaying its one unchanging opinion about the time.

At the station café, a woman named Mara began noticing small disturbances.

Customers stayed longer because they no longer heard the bell reminding them to leave. Others arrived early, suspicious of their watches. A retired geography teacher missed his usual train, though he wore two watches and carried a phone. “It’s not the information,” he told Mara, stirring a coffee that needed no stirring. “I have the information. It’s the permission.”

“Permission for what?”

“To stop doing one thing and start doing another.”

After that, Mara listened differently to the silences between cups touching saucers.

She had inherited the café from her father, along with three good knives, a temperamental refrigerator, and his conviction that every customer should be greeted before being asked what they wanted. For years, the clock had divided her working day into manageable pieces. Seven meant the first rush. Ten meant a quiet breakfast standing behind the counter. Three meant schoolchildren buying buns with coins warm from their pockets. Six meant wiping tables while her father, and later nobody, counted the till. Without the bell, afternoons spread unevenly. Some lasted minutes. Others seemed to contain entire unsuccessful versions of her life.

One Thursday, an elderly man entered carrying a wooden box tied with blue cord. He ordered tea and asked whether anyone had been up to look at the clock.

“Several people,” Mara said. “They all came down looking expensive.”

He smiled but did not explain himself.

When his tea arrived, he opened the box. Inside lay tiny drawers, screwdrivers, a folded cloth, and instruments whose purposes Mara could not guess. He took out a watch, listened to it, and wound it twice.

“Are you the specialist?” she asked.

“No,” he said. “I used to be his brother.”

Mara waited. Years of serving strangers had taught her that questions sometimes closed a conversation more firmly than silence.

“He died in February,” the man said. “On the island. I found the council’s letters when I went through his things.”

Outside, a train arrived with the tired metallic complaint of brakes.

“Can you repair it?”

“I don’t know. He understood large things. I worked on watches.”

“But you came.”

“Yes.”

He drank his tea carefully, holding the cup with both hands. Mara wrapped two sandwiches in paper and gave him the key to the tower.

For three days, nothing happened that anyone could see. The man climbed the tower each morning and returned in the late afternoon, bringing down dust on his shoulders. His name was Elias. He liked mustard, disliked the café’s radio, and sometimes spoke about his brother as though they had quarreled that morning. They had, in fact, quarreled twenty-two years earlier. Neither could remember what had started it, but both had maintained the disagreement with admirable consistency. Once, while Mara washed cups, Elias said, “You can become very skilled at keeping something broken.” She let the water run a moment longer.

On Sunday, he asked Mara to come upstairs.

The tower smelled of iron, cold wood, and old bird nests. Inside the clock, wheels stood taller than dinner plates. Cables descended into darkness. The machinery looked less like an instrument than a small, sleeping factory.

Elias pointed to a worn part resting on his cloth.

“I can replace this,” he said. “But there’s damage elsewhere. It won’t keep perfect time.”

“How imperfect?”

“A minute, perhaps two, over a week.”

Mara looked through the narrow window. Below, a woman was helping a child fasten a coat.

“Neither does anyone,” she said.

The bell sounded at four that afternoon.

It startled a cyclist, interrupted a wedding photograph, and caused the geography teacher to spill soup on his newspaper. In the café, six people looked up simultaneously. Mara, carrying a tray, stopped so abruptly that coffee slid into two saucers.

The sound was not quite as she remembered it. There was a roughness at its edge, a slight unevenness that might always have been there. She had expected to feel her father’s presence when it returned. Instead, she noticed that table four needed clearing and that someone at the counter was smiling.

Elias left the next morning. Mara put sandwiches beside his tea, and this time he paid for them before she could object. She watched him cross the platform carrying his wooden box. The clock said eight; her phone said two minutes after. She decided not to reset it yet. When the train had gone, she returned to the café and found the geography teacher waiting outside. He had forgotten his book and wanted another coffee. Mara unlocked the door, turned on the lights, and asked whether he had caught his train yesterday. “Eventually,” he said, taking off his coat.
